"Some time passed before I recovered enough to attend to the balloon's routine needs. When I finally examined it carefully, I was immensely relieved to find no damage. All my equipment was safe, and fortunately I had lost neither supplies nor ballast. I had secured everything so firmly that such a loss was, in fact, impossible. My watch showed six o'clock. I was still rising quickly, and the barometer indicated an altitude of three and three-quarter miles. Directly beneath me on the ocean lay a small, dark, slightly elongated object, apparently about the size and shape of a child's domino. Through the telescope I clearly identified it as a British ninety-four-gun ship, sailing close to the wind and pitching heavily, with its bow pointed west-southwest. Apart from this ship, I could see only the ocean, the sky, and the sun, which had risen some time before.

"It is time I explained to Your Excellencies the purpose of this dangerous voyage. You will remember that my desperate circumstances in Rotterdam had finally led me to decide on suicide. I did not actually hate life itself; rather, the misfortunes surrounding my situation had tormented me beyond endurance. In this state, still wanting to live but weary of life, I found a new possibility in the treatise at the bookseller's stall. Then I made my final decision. I would depart yet remain alive, leave the world yet continue to exist. To abandon riddles and speak plainly, I resolved to attempt a passage to the moon, whatever the consequences. So that you will not consider me madder than I truly am, I shall explain as well as I can the reasoning that persuaded me such an undertaking, though unquestionably difficult and dangerous, was not entirely beyond the reach of a courageous spirit.

"The first consideration was the moon's actual distance from the earth. The mean, or average, distance between the centres of the two planets is 59.9643 times the earth's equatorial radius, which is only about 237,000 miles. I emphasize that this is the average distance. Remember that the moon follows an elliptical orbit, whose eccentricity amounts to no less than 0.05484 of the ellipse's semimajor axis, with the earth's centre at one focus. If I could somehow arrange to meet the moon at its perigee, the distance I have given would therefore be considerably reduced.

Do you return here often?"

"I have not been back since."

"Neither have I."

As the moon rose, I remembered that tranquil gaze upon the white ceiling, now gone forever. As the moon rose, I remembered the hand pressing mine when I spoke the final words he heard in this world.

It was Estella who next ended our silence.

"So often I have wished and planned to return, but one circumstance after another prevented me. Poor old place—poor, poor place!"

The moon's earliest rays fell upon the silver mist and upon the tears slipping from her eyes. Unaware that I had noticed, and striving to master them, she spoke softly.

"As you were walking here, did you wonder why it had been left like this?"

"Yes, Estella."

"The land is mine. It is the one possession I have never surrendered. Everything else slipped away from me by degrees, but I held on to this. Through all those unhappy years, this was the one thing about which I made a determined stand."

"Will something be built here?"

"Yes, at last. I came to say farewell before it changes. And you," she asked, with an interest in her voice that touched a wanderer's heart, "you still live abroad?"

"I do."

"And prosper, I am sure?"

"I work rather hard to earn enough, and therefore—yes, I prosper."

"I have thought of you often," Estella said.

"Have you really?"

"Very often lately. For a long, difficult period I shut away the memory of what I had discarded without understanding its value. But since acknowledging that memory no longer conflicted with my duty, I have allowed it room in my heart."

"Your place in my heart has never changed," I replied.

Again we fell silent, until she continued.

"I never imagined," Estella said, "that in bidding farewell to this place I would also bid farewell to you. I am very glad of it."

"Glad that we must part again, Estella? Parting is painful to me. The thought of our last farewell has always brought me sorrow and pain."

"But you told me then," she answered with great earnestness, "'God bless you, and God forgive you!' If you could say that then, surely you can say it now, when suffering has taught me more powerfully than anything else, and made me understand the heart you once offered. I have been bent and broken, but I hope that I have taken a better form.

When I review the dreadful list of my offences, I can scarcely believe myself the being whose mind was once possessed by lofty and transcendent dreams of goodness in all its beauty and grandeur. Yet so it is: the fallen angel turns into a malicious fiend. Even that adversary of man and God, however, had companions and allies amid his desolation. I have none.

"You call Frankenstein your friend and appear acquainted with my crimes and his calamities. Yet in recounting them he could never convey the months and hours of wretchedness I endured, consumed by powerless passions. While I ruined his hopes, I fulfilled none of my own longings. They remained fierce and unsatisfied. I still yearned for love and companionship, and still met rejection. Was that not unjust? Must I alone be judged a criminal when the whole human race wronged me? Why do you feel no hatred for Felix, who contemptuously expelled his friend from his doorway? Why not curse the countryman who tried to kill his child's rescuer? No, these are pure and virtuous creatures! I, forsaken and miserable, am a monstrous failure, fit only to be scorned, kicked, and crushed underfoot. Even now the memory of that injustice makes my blood burn.

"Yet I am indeed a wretch. I have killed the beautiful and defenceless, strangled innocent sleepers, and squeezed the life from a throat belonging to one who had never harmed me or any living creature. My creator, that chosen example of all in mankind deserving admiration and love, I condemned to suffering and pursued into ruin beyond repair. He lies there now, pale and cold in death. You loathe me, but your disgust cannot rival my own. I regard the hands that performed these deeds and remember the heart that conceived them, longing for the hour when the sight of these hands and the imagining of those acts shall torment me no longer.

"Do not fear that I shall cause further harm. My task is almost finished. To close the course of my existence and fulfil what remains, neither your death nor any other man's is required, only mine. Do not suppose I will hesitate over that sacrifice. I shall leave your ship upon the raft of ice that carried me here and travel to the globe's northernmost limit. There I shall gather my funeral pyre and burn this wretched body into ash, so that its remnants offer no instruction to some curious, impious creature who might attempt to create another such as I.
